memories.memory_text: I stepped into the apartment block, aware of the weight of my presence—how the light caught my silhouette, how his gaze followed. I didn’t turn, but I felt it.
I kicked off my shoes, slipped off my panties, and lifted my dress over my head in one move—lying back on the bed, I reached up toward Jack and said, 'Amore?'
I saw him there in the bar, ordering coffee, trying to watch someone outside without being noticed—but the glass gave him away. Our eyes met for just a moment before he looked away.
I felt his mouth on me, and my fingers tightened in his hair—not to pull him away, but to hold him there, even though I knew I shouldn’t let him kiss me like that.
He put me in a position I resisted at first, and then I let him—then he kissed me on the lips, deeply, and I didn’t turn away, not that time, and I came without meaning to.
I saw him wince when we bumped—something was wrong, and he couldn’t hide it, not from me. When I asked about his pain, he finally admitted it: a broken rib.
After he refused the hospital, I offered to get him strong coffee instead—my eyes must have sparkled, because I knew just the place, and suddenly it felt like a moment we’d remember.
I introduced Jack to Anna as Signor Farfalla, my butterfly man, and I could feel my eyes sparkling with mischief as I said it—like we shared a secret the others couldn’t touch.

I slid my chair close and let my knee press against Jack’s under the table—just enough to feel the warmth—then smiled at him, and he smiled back, and for a moment it was only us, even with Anna right there.
I asked Eduardo if he’d like to have a drink soon, letting the words come out just as I’d practiced—casual, open, but with Monday already fixed in my mind.
I pretended to forget our usual place, watching him closely—then lit up at Locanda Grapelli, as if it were the perfect choice, and locked in seven o’clock with a question in my eyes.
I remember Jack taking such care with his clothes that evening, like every button and fold mattered more than usual—perhaps for me.
I kissed him and said I didn’t think you would come—my voice was unsteady, and I felt the weight of breaking my own rules just by saying it.

I repeated my order in clear, measured Italian, making sure the waiter heard every word—non gasata, per favore—after he ignored me and spoke only to Jack. He finally nodded, properly this time, and I felt the shift: I was in control.

Jack bought me a rose from the gypsy, not because we're a couple, but to keep the illusion alive for a little longer. I took it, smiled, and said in Italian—'As long as we know it is an illusion'—and for a moment, the warmth between us felt real, even if it wasn't.

I stepped out of the bathroom and saw Jack lying there, so still—too still—and the drawer to my purse closed just a second too fast. I didn’t say anything, but I felt the air change, like something unspoken had already been taken from me.
I was in the cafe, sitting across from a young Italian man in a suit. He showed me photographs. I stayed serious. He left, and I was gone when he was out of sight.

I kissed him under the tree, my purse in hand, the weight of the watermelon at my feet—his lips responded, but not quite like before, and I wondered, just for a second, why the hesitation in his breath.
I asked if it was farther, and when Jack said ten kilometers—another twenty minutes—I paused to calculate: twelve kilometers in twenty minutes didn’t make sense, not at this speed.
I asked Jack where we were going, and my voice came out sharper than I meant—it startled me how narrow the track was, how far from the road.
I laughed and said 'Not with you,' but even as I spoke, I felt the car lurch over the stones, my hands gripping the door and seat—my fingers still remember how tightly I held on.

I asked him if Edward was his real name, and when he said yes, I didn’t believe him—I watched his hands behind the basket, hidden, and when I reached for my purse, I heard that click. My breath caught, but I kept my face still.

I took the suntan lotion from my purse and rubbed it over my body slowly—my breasts, my belly, my thighs—then offered it to him, saying, 'Will you put this on my back?' My voice was calm, but I watched him, waiting to see if he would move, if he would break.
I took my shoe from Jack and said, 'Grazie, Eduardo,' the words slipping out before I could stop them.

I told him about the gun—how one of the girls gave it to me after the second woman was killed in Chieti. Madonna, Eduardo, I said, shivering, because I still see those photos, and I don't understand how someone could do that.
I heard Jack shout 'CLARA!' up at my window after he ran to my apartment and rang the buzzer twice.
I saw Jack across the square, just standing there, looking for me—so I raised my hand and waved, then stepped down from the steps toward him, letting the crowd close around me.
I kissed Jack, feeling the warmth of the sun and the quiet between us, not knowing the crosshairs had found his head.
I shouted 'Forever?' and when he said 'Forever,' I swore in Italian and threw my arms around Jack, holding him tight. I told him, 'I love you, Signor Eduardo Farfalla.'

One second I was holding Jack, tears in my eyes, and the next—there was a terrible noise, a burst like metal tearing, and Mathilde screamed. I saw her hands, blood everywhere, and I didn't understand what had just happened.

His name isn't Eduardo. He told me, 'My name is Jack,' and I just repeated it—'Jack'—like I was trying to hold the sound of it in my mouth, as if the name itself could explain why my chest suddenly felt tight.

He gave me a sealed envelope with money and said, 'Look after it. In case.' I asked, 'In case?' but he didn't finish—just looked at me like he wanted to say something final, something heavy, and then told me to go.

memories.memory_text: I felt Ingrid's arms wrap around me, her skin warm against my back, as we sat together watching the fire—her breath steady beside my ear, the whiskey sharp on my tongue, and the weight of years pressing down.

I saw a branch dip and snow fall. I pulled Ingrid down and covered with her. I pulled the Walther from my pocket, cocked it, and waited. I saw blue smoke, then fired three shots into the trees. I heard a groan. I checked the man—he was dead. I found a military ID in his pocket. Ingrid asked who he was. I said a hunter.

She started walking back to call the police. I watched her go. Then I raised the gun and shot her once in the neck. She fell like something hunted. I stepped over her without looking down. Her blood spread into the fur of her collar—white, then red. I didn’t turn back.
I smashed the CB radio and pulled the distributor cap from the Mercedes, burying it deep in the snow so no one could track or use it.
I got into the Saab and started moving—ferry to Gotland, changed clothes and boats in Ystad, drove to Trelleborg, then the night crossing to Travemunde, on to Hamburg, and caught a train from there.
I took the envelope from Larry and slipped it into my inside pocket without looking at it. The final payment from the Stockholm account was done, and I didn’t need to count it—he wouldn’t be wrong.

Larry slid a mobile phone in a cellophane bag across the table and told me to get to Castelvecchio and stay there. I remember the weight of the cigarette in my hand, the silence after he said 'Do nothing till you get my call.'
I looked at the sign, then up at the town—silent, with dark windows and crumbling roofs. After the dog barked and the wind hissed, I decided to leave. I drove away without another look.
I opened the window and tossed the phone—sealed in cellophane—out into the ravine. It fell fast, disappearing into the drop below.
I set up the Leica binoculars from my holdall and scanned Castelvecchio in grid formation, checking for movement—just an old man, a woman, a dog. The town looked empty.
I moved through the town photographing each section in a grid, making sure nothing was missed, the way I always do.
I photographed each of the four alleyways at the crossroads, making sure to capture the angles and inclines—useful for navigation, no unnecessary detail.

I heard a dog barking from one of the alleyways—no dog in sight—but the sound grew louder when I turned back, leading me to a narrow gap in the stone that looked like a crack, not a passage. I slipped through.

I stood at the pay phone in the square, lighting a cigarette while Larry’s voice told me this job would make me free—after this, I could walk away. I didn’t answer right away, just turned the word over in my head, feeling the weight of it.
I sorted the photographs of Castel del Monte into street plans and two types of exit routes—by car and on foot—making sure each category was clear and separate.
I took apart my Walther PPK/S, cleaned each component, and applied oil to ensure it would function without failure.

I said 'Amidst gathering clouds' to test the recognition signal, and when she responded with that stiff talk about weather and boarding school, I knew it was code—her words were too forced to be casual.
I ordered a strawberry gelato and confirmed my alias as Edward. The sun was high, and the café was warming up by midday.
I was dreaming, the book slipping from my hand—then the thud, my eyes open, Walther in hand, aimed at the door before I even thought.
I sat at the café where I met Mathilde, watching the post office entrance. After an hour with no movement, I left the exact change on the table and stood up.
I studied the parts laid out on the floor—the receiver, bolt, barrel—waiting until the final piece made it complete. I noticed the serial number had been scratched off before I touched anything.
I assembled the weapon piece by piece, then snuggled the buttpad to my shoulder and looked down the barrel, feeling the weight and alignment. I slowly squeezed the trigger as the world cut out.

I studied the photo of Father Benedetto with that heavyset Italian man—Fabio—his arm around him like family, and when the priest noticed, he said some sheep are dearer, especially the ones who've strayed. He called Fabio a 'car doctor,' but in a way that made it clear it wasn't just about cars.

He asked if I ever wanted to be anything other than a photographer. He said my hands were for a craftsman, not an artist, and that I’d said the opposite before. When he looked at my Rolex, I stayed quiet.
I followed Fabio through the metal door into a cluttered workshop where a blue Alfa Romeo was being resprayed white, and a Lancia was half-welded to another—parts not meant to go together, now fused.
I took the tools and a damaged gearwheel from Fabio’s garage, wrapping the gear in oily newspaper before putting it in my bag. He didn’t care—just grinned and said 'Niente!' when I asked how much.
At the door, I saw a photograph on the notice board—Fabio as a boy, maybe fourteen, in an AS Roma strip, with Father Benedetto’s arm around him. I didn’t say anything. Just nodded and left.
I placed the gearwheel on the stone floor and struck it with the mallet, breaking it into five pieces while the church bells rang overhead.

I filed the connectors, adjusted the sight mountings, and fine-tuned the suppressor until the trigger pull was smooth—then balanced the rifle on the ruler’s edge. It held true at the mark, perfectly level.
I saw a lone man near the payphone who didn't fit—too visible, not local, not Company. I ran through the possibilities: cop, Joe, shooter—but nothing lined up. He was just... wrong.
Larry offered help, but I told him I could handle it. When he said I sounded spooked, I said it was the line. I didn't need backup. I made the call to act alone.
I heard Larry say they were moving the drop, and something in his voice made me tighten my grip on the phone—I kept scanning the road, the lake, the tree line, but nothing felt right.
When Larry mentioned a breach, I paused—I didn't know about any breach, and that silence before I asked 'What breach?' was the first time I felt the plan slipping.
I pulled the car to the curb and saw Clara standing there with the red purse, the blue bag at her feet. She leaned in, kissed me long and full on the lips—then I told her to put the bags in the back.
I found Clara's shoe near the car and handed it back to her without a word. I remember staring at it, wondering if this was the moment I started losing my grip—or finally gaining something real.
